objects: variant discovery; SNP-based heritability; phenotype prediction
conclusion: Separate models for discovery, heritability estimation and prediction cause inefficiency and power loss; the proposed mixture model addresses these tasks jointly.
scope: Motivation and intended capabilities; no universal optimality theorem.
span: Gene discovery, estimation of heritability captured by SNP arrays, inference on genetic architecture and prediction analyses of complex traits are usually performed using different statistical models and methods, leading to inefficiency and loss of power. Here we use a Bayesian mixture model that simultaneously allows variant discovery, estimation of genetic variance explained by all variants and prediction of unobserved phenotypes in new samples.

conclusion: The sampling model is additive linear regression y = 1_n mu + X beta + epsilon with Gaussian residual covariance I sigma_e^2.
scope: Statistical framework for the fitted marker effects.
span: Phenotypes are related to markers with a standard linear regression model y = 1_{n} μ + X β + ε , where y is a n-dimensional vector of phenotypes, 1 n is a n-dimensional vector of ones, μ is the general mean, X is an n×p matrix of genotypes encoded as 0, 1 or 2 copies of a reference allele. The vector β is a p-dimensional vector of SNP effects and ε is a n-dimensional vector of residuals, ε ∼ N ( 0 , I σ_{e}^{2} ) with I being a n×n identity matrix.

conclusion: Residuals are jointly Gaussian with mean zero and covariance I sigma_e^2.

assumptions: mixture weights positive and summing to one; relative component variances fixed
conclusion: SNP effects have a four-component zero-mean normal mixture with variances (0, 1E-4, 1E-3, 1E-2) sigma_g^2; the zero-variance component supplies sparsity.
scope: Specified prior family; mixture grid is a modeling choice rather than a data property.
span: We followed Erbe et al. [8] and a priori assumed a mixture of four zero mean normal distributions, where the relative variance for each mixture component is fixed: p ( β_{j} | π , σ_{g}^{2} ) = π_{1} × N ( 0 , 0 × σ_{g}^{2} ) + π_{2} × N ( 0 , 10^{− 4} × σ_{g}^{2} ) + π_{3} × N ( 0 , 10^{− 3} × σ_{g}^{2} ) + π_{4} × N ( 0 , 10^{− 2} × σ_{g}^{2} ) . Here, σ_{g}^{2} is the additive genetic variance explained by SNPs. Sparseness is included into the model by setting the effect and variance of the first mixture component to zero.

conclusion: Posterior fitting uses Gibbs sampling from the full conditional distribution of each unknown parameter.
scope: MCMC procedure; this statement supplies no finite-run accuracy or convergence guarantee.
span: MCMC estimation of the unknown parameters ( μ , π , β , σ_{g}^{2} , σ_{e}^{2} ) used a Gibbs scheme to sample values from each unknown parameter’s conditional posterior distribution. Details of the sampling procedure are outlined in S1 Text.

conclusion: Model parameters are summarized by posterior sample means, and a marker PIP is the proportion of iterations in which it is included.
scope: Posterior model summaries and association evidence; PIP does not itself identify unobserved causal variants.
span: After having generated samples from the posterior distributions model parameters are estimated by the sample means of their posterior probabilities respectively. Estimates of are averages over different regression models drawn conditional on different model vectors, known as “Bayesian model averaging”. The posterior inclusion probability (PIP), defined as the proportion of iterations that included a specific marker in the model, was used as a measure of the ability of the model to identify associated SNPs.

objects: observed SNP effects; unobserved causal variants; LD
assumptions: causal variants can be unobserved and correlated with genotyped SNPs
conclusion: Inferred SNP effects and architecture describe observed SNPs; unknown correlations with causal variants affect interpretation of causal architecture.
scope: Observed-marker inference rather than direct causal-variant inference.
span: In addition to the caveats relating to the specific mixture model we emphasize that the inference drawn on SNP effects and genetic architecture is from observed SNPs and not on the causal variants directly. The true but unknown pattern of correlation between unobserved causal variants and genotyped SNPs will impact the inference about genetic architecture.

objects: SNP effect updates; MCMC cycle; 500 nonzero effects
conclusion: The reduced scheme then updates SNPs in random order until 500 nonzero effects have been sampled, retaining previous effects for SNPs not updated.
scope: Described computational shortcut; equality with the full posterior is not established in this span.
span: For the first 5,000 cycles the effect of each SNP was sampled per iteration. After this we did not sample all SNPs in each MCMC iteration, but updated SNP effects (in random order) only until we had sampled 500 SNPs with non-zero effects. SNPs not updated in the current iteration kept their effect sizes from the previous MCMC cycle.
